claim: The Drosophila wing imaginal disc pouch region is planar and ellipsoidal to a good approximation.
source: To a good approximation, this region is planar and ellipsoidal.
evidence: This is a descriptive statement about the geometry of the wing disc pouch region based on the authors' observations.

claim: Cells near the center of the wing disc pouch have smaller cell areas and are more isotropic in shape.
source: Cells near the center have smaller cell areas and are more isotropic in shape, whereas cells near the periphery have larger cell areas and are elongated tangentially (Aegerter-Wilmsen et al., 2010; Legoff et al., 2013; Mao et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by both the current study's data and citations to previous work.

claim: Cells near the periphery of the wing disc pouch have larger cell areas and are elongated tangentially.
source: Cells near the center have smaller cell areas and are more isotropic in shape, whereas cells near the periphery have larger cell areas and are elongated tangentially (Aegerter-Wilmsen et al., 2010; Legoff et al., 2013; Mao et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by both the current study's data and citations to previous work.

claim: Tangentially oriented bonds of elongated cells in the periphery are under higher tension than radially oriented bonds.
source: Cell shape has been correlated with mechanical stress: tangentially oriented bonds of elongated cells in the periphery are under higher tension than radially oriented bonds (Legoff et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Differential proliferation could generate patterns of cell morphology in the wing pouch if the center grows faster than the rest.
source: It has been previously proposed that this pattern of cell morphology in the wing pouch could stem from differential proliferation: if the center grows faster than the rest, the resulting area pressure could stretch peripheral cells tangentially (Mao et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a previously proposed hypothesis cited from the literature.

claim: Cell rearrangements occur in the wing disc during development.
source: However, it has since been shown that cell rearrangements occur (Dye et al., 2017; Heller et al., 2016), which could relax stress patterns once growth has become uniform.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Cell rearrangements could relax stress patterns once growth has become uniform.
source: However, it has since been shown that cell rearrangements occur (Dye et al., 2017; Heller et al., 2016), which could relax stress patterns once growth has become uniform.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the known behavior of cell rearrangements.

claim: Stress patterns may relax during homogeneous growth in the absence of cell rearrangements.
source: Furthermore, stress patterns may even relax during homogeneous growth in the absence of cell rearrangements (Ranft et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The pattern of tangential cell elongation becomes stronger over time during mid-third larval instar.
source: We quantify the pattern of tangential cell elongation and show that it becomes stronger over time, even though growth is spatially uniform and cell rearrangements are frequent.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Growth is spatially uniform during mid-third larval instar.
source: We quantify the pattern of tangential cell elongation and show that it becomes stronger over time, even though growth is spatially uniform and cell rearrangements are frequent.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Cell rearrangements are frequent during mid-third larval instar.
source: We quantify the pattern of tangential cell elongation and show that it becomes stronger over time, even though growth is spatially uniform and cell rearrangements are frequent.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The change in tangential cell elongation is coupled to a radially biased pattern of cell neighbor exchanges.
source: Strikingly, this change in tangential cell elongation is coupled to a radially biased pattern of cell neighbor exchanges.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Active patterning of radial cell neighbor exchanges can account for the observed morphology patterns in the absence of differential growth.
source: Using a physical model of tissue dynamics, we show that active patterning of radial cell neighbor exchanges can account for the observed morphology patterns in the absence of differential growth.
evidence: This claim is supported by the theoretical model presented in the manuscript.

claim: Negative values of Qrr correspond to tangential elongation.
source: The negative value corresponds to tangential elongation (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a definition of the measurement convention used in the study.

claim: The radial gradients in cell area and elongation grow slightly more pronounced over time during the timelapse.
source: When evaluated over the timelapse, we find that these radial gradients grow slightly more pronounced over time (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C–D.

claim: Tissue area growth is to a good approximation independent of the distance to the center.
source: These data show that tissue area growth, as well as cell division rate, are to a good approximation independent of the distance to the center.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Cell division rate is to a good approximation independent of the distance to the center.
source: These data show that tissue area growth, as well as cell division rate, are to a good approximation independent of the distance to the center.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 1.

claim: The radial component of tissue shear is small.
source: The radial component of tissue shear is small, and cell divisions do not contribute to radial tissue shear.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: Cell divisions do not contribute to radial tissue shear.
source: The radial component of tissue shear is small, and cell divisions do not contribute to radial tissue shear.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: There is a pronounced buildup of a tangential pattern of cell elongation accompanied by a radial pattern of T1 transitions and of correlation effects.
source: In contrast, we observe a pronounced buildup of a tangential pattern of cell elongation accompanied by a radial pattern of T1 transitions and of correlation effects.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 2.

claim: Pressure increases toward the center of the wing disc.
source: From our data, we can also infer the radial profile of tissue area pressure, revealing that pressure increases toward the center (Figure 4D and Appendix 1 part 3).
evidence: This claim is inferred from laser ablation data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The pattern of tangential cell elongation persists after RNAi knockdown of both fat and dachs.
source: Nonetheless, the pattern of tangential cell elongation persists to the end of larval development (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The radial profiles of cell elongation in ft+d RNAi and control wings are similar when using scaled coordinates.
source: Using scaled coordinates, we find that the radial profiles of cell elongation in ft+d RNAi and control wings are similar (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The cell elongation pattern in the pk mutant is similar to the wild-type control.
source: We found that the cell elongation pattern in the pk mutant is similar to the wild-type control (Figure 5E–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E–I.

claim: In the pk mutant, the region of tangential cell elongation extends even further into the center than in control wings.
source: In the pk mutant, the region of tangential cell elongation extends even further into the center than in control wings.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The tangential cell elongation pattern persists in the absence of either PCP pathway.
source: We conclude that the tangential cell elongation pattern persists in the absence of either PCP pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on PCP pathway perturbations.

claim: The anisotropic cue can be locally generated by mechanosensitive self-organization and does not require the existence of pre-patterned polarity cues.
source: By this mechanism, the anisotropic cue introduced earlier in our model can be locally generated by mechanosensitive self-organization and does not require the existence of pre-patterned polarity cues.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the theoretical model.

claim: A clear reduction in the magnitude of tangential cell elongation is observed after MyoVI RNAi compared to wild type.
source: We observe a clear reduction in the magnitude of tangential cell elongation as compared to wild type at this stage (Figure 7A–D, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Reduction of MyoVI levels results in increased cell area in the wing.
source: In addition, our model predicts that such reduction of cell elongation would result in an increase of cell area in the wing (Equations 1-6). The observed pattern of increased cell area upon reducing MyoVI levels with RNAi is consistent with this prediction (Figure 7E–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E–F and is consistent with model predictions.

claim: MyoVI is involved in Rho-dependent activation of actin-myosin cytoskeleton.
source: Our data, together with the fact that MyoVI is involved in Rho-dependent activation of actin-myosin cytoskeleton (Acharya et al., 2018), suggest that MyoVI is a molecular component of the mechanosensitive feedback we describe in our self-organized model.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: MyoVI is a molecular component of the mechanosensitive feedback described in the self-organized model.
source: Our data, together with the fact that MyoVI is involved in Rho-dependent activation of actin-myosin cytoskeleton (Acharya et al., 2018), suggest that MyoVI is a molecular component of the mechanosensitive feedback we describe in our self-organized model.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from combining experimental data with known molecular functions.

claim: MyoII can polarize in response to exogenous stress in a Rho-dependent manner in wing disc stretching experiments.
source: Also, wing disc stretching experiments have shown that MyoII can polarize in response to exogenous stress in a Rho-dependent manner (Duda et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The region around the DV boundary has a different ratio of elastic constants than the rest of the tissue.
source: Lastly, our laser ablation analysis shows that the region around the DV boundary has a different ratio of elastic constants than the rest of the tissue, which could affect the self-organized pattern formation we describe.
evidence: This claim is supported by laser ablation data presented earlier in the manuscript.

claim: The compound eye of Drosophila consists of hundreds of ommatidia organized in a precise hexagonal array that is required to fully sample the visual field.
source: For example, the compound eye of Drosophila consists of hundreds of ommatidia organized in a precise hexagonal array that is required to fully sample the visual field (Kumar, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Spatial patterns of cell morphology emerge during growth of the Drosophila larval imaginal discs.
source: For example, spatial patterns of cell morphology emerge during growth of the Drosophila larval imaginal discs, which are precursors of adult tissues (Aegerter-Wilmsen et al., 2010; Condic et al., 1991; Legoff et al., 2013; Mao et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Cell morphology patterns have been proposed to be involved in the eversion process during the larva to pupa transition.
source: These patterns have been proposed to be involved in the eversion process, during which these flattened epithelial sacs turn themselves inside out when the animal transitions from larva to pupa (Condic et al., 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The wing disc pouch region is the precursor of the adult wing blade.
source: We focus specifically on the cell shape patterns in the central 'pouch' region, which is the precursor of the adult wing blade.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila development.

claim: Ecadherin-GFP was used as an apical junction marker.
source: We used Ecadherin-GFP as an apical junction marker (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: The pattern of tangential cell elongation is interrupted around the Dorsal-Ventral (DV) boundary, where cells are elongated parallel to this boundary.
source: It also reveals that this pattern is interrupted around the Dorsal-Ventral (DV) boundary, where cells are elongated parallel to this boundary (red in Figure 1C).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The Anterior-Posterior (AP) boundary affects cell morphology, but the effect is weaker and more variable at this stage.
source: The Anterior-Posterior (AP) boundary also affects cell morphology (Landsberg et al., 2009), but the effect is weaker and more variable at this stage; thus, we do not quantify it separately.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data combined with a citation to previous work.

claim: Tissue growth results from a combination of cell division, cell area changes, and cell extrusions.
source: Cell division rate has been previously used as an indicator of growth; however, tissue growth actually results from a combination of cell division, cell area changes, and cell extrusions (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is established knowledge about tissue growth mechanics.

claim: Tissue shear can be decomposed into contributions from cell divisions, cell elongation changes, T1 transitions, and correlation effects.
source: Tissue shear can be decomposed into contributions from cell divisions, cell elongation changes, T1 transitions, and so-called correlation effects (Etournay et al., 2015; Merkel et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a methodological approach established in previous work.

claim: Correlation effects result mainly from correlated fluctuations in cell elongation and cell rotation.
source: Here, correlation effects result mainly from correlated fluctuations in cell elongation and cell rotation (see Appendix 3 and Merkel et al., 2017).
evidence: This is explained in the manuscript and supported by a citation.

claim: The spatial patterns of tissue growth and its cellular contributions exhibit overall anisotropies perpendicular to the DV boundary.
source: We find that the spatial patterns of tissue growth and its cellular contributions exhibit overall anisotropies perpendicular to the DV boundary, as reported previously (Dye et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data that is consistent with previous work.

claim: The patterns of cell elongation changes and T1 transitions can be described as a superposition of a uniformly oriented pattern and an approximately radial or tangential pattern.
source: In addition, the patterns of cell elongation changes and T1 transitions can be described as a superposition of a uniformly oriented pattern and an approximately radial or tangential pattern (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: This is an observation and interpretation of the experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The model can account for the observed pattern of cell area.
source: Finally, we show that this function can account for the observed pattern of cell area (see Figure 3G).
evidence: This is a result from comparing the model predictions to experimental data.

claim: Local average cell elongation correlates well with the principal direction of shear stress.
source: We find that local average cell elongation correlates well with the principal direction of shear stress.
evidence: This is an observation from the laser ablation experiments.

claim: Cells in the band around the DV boundary have different mechanical properties than elsewhere in the tissue.
source: Also, we observe that the cells in the band around the DV boundary, which are exposed to high Wg and Notch signaling, have different mechanical properties than elsewhere in the tissue.
evidence: This is an observation from the laser ablation experiments.

claim: Near the DV boundary, cells elongate less than outside this region for comparable amounts of stress.
source: Near the DV boundary, cells elongate less than outside this region for comparable amounts of stress (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,E).
evidence: This is an observation from the laser ablation experiments shown in the figures.

claim: The relationship between cell elongation and stress normalized by the elastic modulus has a slope 1 in the absence of polarity-driven stress.
source: The relationship between cell elongation and stress normalized by the elastic modulus has a slope 1 in the absence of polarity-driven stress (see Equation 2).
evidence: This is a prediction from the theoretical model.

claim: A much smaller slope is observed for the relationship between cell elongation and normalized stress in the experimental data, indicating that polarity-driven stress is significant.
source: We observe a much smaller slope for this relationship in our data (Figure 4C), indicating that polarity-driven stress is significant.
evidence: This is an observation from the laser ablation experiments that is interpreted using the model.

claim: The stress profile in the wing disc is consistent with the observed measurements of both cell elongation and area.
source: In sum, we find a stress profile in the wing disc that is consistent with the observed measurements of both cell elongation and area.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing laser ablation data with cell morphology measurements.

claim: Fat and Core are two well-characterized PCP pathways.
source: There are two well-characterized PCP pathways: Fat and Core (Butler and Wallingford, 2017; Eaton, 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In the wing, the Fat and Core PCP systems form tissue-scale polarity patterns during growth.
source: In the wing, these systems form tissue-scale polarity patterns during growth (Brittle et al., 2012; Merkel et al., 2014; Sagner et al., 2012) and are required to position the hairs and cuticle ridges on the adult wing (Adler et al., 1998; Doyle et al., 2008; Eaton, 2003; Gubb and García-Bellido, 1982; Hogan et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The Fat and Core PCP pathways are required to position the hairs and cuticle ridges on the adult wing.
source: In the wing, these systems form tissue-scale polarity patterns during growth (Brittle et al., 2012; Merkel et al., 2014; Sagner et al., 2012) and are required to position the hairs and cuticle ridges on the adult wing (Adler et al., 1998; Doyle et al., 2008; Eaton, 2003; Gubb and García-Bellido, 1982; Hogan et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: RNAi targeting both fat and dachs results in almost complete loss of Dachsous from the apical membrane.
source: This perturbation results in almost complete loss of Dachsous from the apical membrane, and any residual signal is no longer polarized, confirming the loss of PCP (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental validation shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Any residual Dachsous signal after ft+d RNAi is no longer polarized.
source: This perturbation results in almost complete loss of Dachsous from the apical membrane, and any residual signal is no longer polarized, confirming the loss of PCP (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental validation shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Suppression of tissue growth is observed upon ft+d double RNAi knockdown.
source: Furthermore, we observe a suppression of tissue growth upon ft+d double RNAi knockdown (visible at the end of larval development in Figure 5A and in the resulting adult wings in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), consistent with previous work on the loss of both Dachs and Fat (Cho and Irvine, 2004).
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments that is consistent with previous work.

claim: MyoVI is encoded by jaguar (jar) in Drosophila.
source: MyoVI, encoded by jaguar (jar) in Drosophila, is an upstream component of a Rho-dependent signaling pathway that reorganizes the actin-myosin cytoskeleton in response to mechanical stress (Acharya et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: MyoVI is an upstream component of a Rho-dependent signaling pathway that reorganizes the actin-myosin cytoskeleton in response to mechanical stress.
source: MyoVI, encoded by jaguar (jar) in Drosophila, is an upstream component of a Rho-dependent signaling pathway that reorganizes the actin-myosin cytoskeleton in response to mechanical stress (Acharya et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Mechanosensation in wing discs involves Rho polarization and signaling.
source: Experiments in wing discs also indicate that mechanosensation involves Rho polarization and signaling (Duda et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The residual pattern of cell elongation after MyoVI removal could be due to polarity existing outside of the perturbed region.
source: Thus, the residual pattern of cell elongation that we observe after removal of MyoVI in the wing pouch could be due to polarity existing outside of this perturbed region.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the experimental observations.

claim: The residual pattern of cell elongation after MyoVI removal could indicate an incomplete knockdown from RNAi or the presence of other mechanosensitive elements in the tissue.
source: In addition, the residual pattern could also indicate an incomplete knockdown from RNAi or the presence of other mechanosensitive elements in the tissue.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the experimental observations.

claim: The mechanosensitive feedback mechanism is a significant determinant of the cell shape patterns in the wing pouch.
source: Nevertheless, given the clear phenotype that is fully consistent with our model, we propose that the mechanosensitive feedback mechanism is a significant determinant of the cell shape patterns in the wing pouch.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results and model predictions.
